Listen to this article Share An opinion article by Ejike Ezejelue Advertisement Advertisement Black Friday Is More Than a Sales Event I have come to see Black Friday as much more than a period of discounts. For an e-commerce business, it is one of the clearest tests of whether the systems behind the storefront can cope when customer demand rises sharply. It tests product selection, inventory planning, people, technology, accounting, packaging and logistics—often at the same time. At Amary Nigeria, our experience during the November 2025 Black Friday campaign brought this reality into sharp focus. It was a very successful campaign. We received more than 12,000 orders during the campaign period, with daily orders routinely exceeding 300 and peaking at around 500. Outside major promotional periods, our normal operating volume is now more than 100 orders a day. The difference in demand meant that success depended on much more than attracting customers. When Demand Outruns Preparation Even with preparation, some products sold much faster than we had anticipated. A few items that attracted attention during the campaign went on to prove themselves as strong-demand products. That is one of the important lessons of Black Friday: it gives businesses real evidence of what customers want, rather than relying only on assumptions, opinions or historical sales. Advertisement At the same time, the surge exposed the risks of inadequate stock planning. We experienced shortages in some products and had to reorder urgently from suppliers. In certain cases, we used faster shipping options even though they were more expensive. We also sourced from alternative local suppliers within Nigeria to keep up with demand. The warehouse came under considerable pressure, and inventory management became more demanding. We increased staff capacity by approximately 100 per cent to support the campaign. The experience showed us that a business cannot treat fulfilment as an afterthought. A customer who has paid for an item expects the business to deliver it accurately and on time. Advertisement The Work Behind Every Order An order is not completed when a customer clicks the buy button. It has to be confirmed, located in the inventory, picked, checked, packaged, documented and handed over for delivery. Each stage requires people, clear processes and reliable information. When order volume rises quickly, weaknesses in any one of those stages can affect the entire operation. Advertisement Advertisement Our experience over more than five years in e-commerce helped us manage the pressure, but experience alone is not a substitute for systems. The campaign exposed gaps in our inventory and fulfilment processes and pushed us to improve how orders move through the warehouse. We focused on faster processing, better packaging and more disciplined shipping procedures. The campaign also influenced our decision to expand warehouse capacity. As the business grew, the space and processes that once worked became less suitable for the volume and variety of goods we were handling. Growth creates new operational demands. Businesses have to recognise those demands early and invest in the capacity required to meet them. More Orders Do Not Always Mean More Profit There is another side of Black Friday that businesses must examine honestly: revenue and order volume do not automatically translate into stronger short-term profitability. Aggressive discounts can reduce margins, while higher volumes bring additional costs in staffing, packaging, sourcing, storage and delivery. A campaign can look impressive on the sales dashboard and still put pressure on the bottom line. Our main objective during the 2025 campaign was to attract customers and grow market share. That objective mattered. Some customers who discovered us during the promotional period continued to buy from us afterwards, including at regular prices. That longer-term customer relationship is part of the value of a successful campaign, even where the immediate margin on discounted orders is lower. But businesses must understand the numbers behind the excitement. Getting 10,000 orders may sound impressive, but 1,000 well-managed, profitable orders can be more valuable to a business. Order volume, revenue, market share and profit all matter, but they do not mean the same thing. Profit is what gives a business the capacity to reinvest, improve its operations and grow sustainably. What Black Friday Teaches E-commerce Businesses First, understand demand. Businesses should study which products customers are searching for, which items are converting and which products are not performing. The information gathered during a major sales period can guide future purchasing decisions, product selection and inventory allocation. Second, visibility matters. Having good products is not enough if customers cannot find them. Businesses need to invest in product presentation, accurate listings, pricing, promotion and the channels through which customers discover their products. Third, prepare the operation, not just the marketing. Inventory, warehouse space, staff capacity, order management, accounting, packaging and logistics should be considered before a campaign begins. This applies whether a business sells through a marketplace or through its own online store. Marketplaces can provide access to customers, but sellers remain responsible for having the stock and operational discipline to fulfil orders. Finally, measure success properly. A business should look beyond the number of orders and ask what those orders contributed after discounts and operating costs. It should also assess customer retention, cancellation and return patterns, fulfilment performance and the lessons that can improve the next campaign. Building for the Next Stage of Growth Amary’s journey reflects how much the business of e-commerce changes as operations expand. We have grown from handling approximately one order a day to processing more than 100 orders daily in normal operations. Our product range has expanded to more than 120 products and product varieties, supported by an inventory of thousands of individual SKUs. We have also grown from operating on one marketplace to having a presence on more than six marketplaces across African markets. Our expansion from Nigeria into Kenya, including operations on Jumia Kenya and Kilimall, has further reinforced the importance of building systems that can work across different markets. Each market has its own customer expectations, logistics realities and operating requirements. Expansion is not simply about listing products in another country; it requires the people, processes, stock and local execution to serve customers reliably. The 2025 Black Friday campaign was successful, but its greatest value was not only the sales it generated. It showed us where demand was strongest, where our operations needed to improve and what capacity we needed for the next stage. Looking Ahead to Black Friday 2026 The lessons from 2025 have informed how we prepared for the 2026 Black Friday campaign. Our priorities are to grow market share, increase order volume and revenue, while maintaining healthy profit margins. The campaign is still underway, and we will wait until it wraps up before assessing the final results. We are looking forward to the campaign reports and hoping for an even stronger outcome. For e-commerce businesses across Africa, that is perhaps the bigger point. Black Friday should not be treated simply as a race to offer the deepest discount or record the largest number of orders. It should be an opportunity to understand customers, strengthen operations and build a business capable of delivering consistently long after the promotional banners have come down. About the Author Ejike Ezejelue is an e-commerce entrepreneur and business operator with more than five years of experience building and managing online retail operations. He is the founder of Amary Nigeria, which has expanded its marketplace operations across African markets, including Kenya. He shares practical insights on e-commerce, business operations and growth.
